item.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
item.description:
Source: www.smithsonianmag.com

Top Comment:

Unfortunately the article does not identify precisely the "miracle" wheat.

"Triticum turgidum" is ambiguous, because this wheat species has many different subspecies, with very different characteristics.

There are 2 important subspecies of "Triticum turgidum", emmer wheat, which was 1 of the 3 cereals domesticated at the beginning of the Neolithic (barley, einkorn wheat and emmer wheat), and durum wheat (a.k.a. pasta wheat or macaroni wheat), which was produced from emmer wheat by a genetic mutation, several thousand years after domestication.

From the article, it is not clear if the discussed wheat is just some cultivar of emmer wheat or it belongs to a more exotic subspecies of "Triticum turgidum".

Any references from the Bible are unlikely to describe anything else but some variety of emmer wheat.

While most wheat-based food is nowadays produced from either hexaploid bread wheat or tetraploid durum wheat, there are on the market various niche products (e.g. some kinds of biscuits) made from spelt wheat, emmer wheat or einkorn wheat (though the product labels frequently confuse the hexaploid spelt wheat with the tetraploid emmer wheat).

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

> exhibited frequent, profound transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. item.title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
item.description:
Source: thedataexchange.media

Top Comment:

I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the generator provably generates the correct mass scale assertions.

This is how formal methods can constrain AI for large systems.

We're doing this at the Open Markets Initiative, where we've generated millions of lines of Lean 4, TLA+, and Rocq that ensure that our open source electronic trading protocol code is accurate. We didn't expect it but the Lean prover did identify some incorrect steps. https://github.com/Open-Markets-Initiative
